source.version: TREW 2024 workshop paper at CHI 2024, revised and accepted 17 April 2024 (p. 8); the ACM Reference Format identifies TREW 2024 on May 11, 2024 (p. 1). Complete eight-page workshop-hosted PDF read in memory on 2026-10-09, including references on pp. 7-8; no appendix is included. No local markdown or PDF was available or created. The remote PDF URL is recorded in pdf_file.
source.title_on_document: Explorations in human vs. generative AI creative performances: A study on human-AI creative potential

paper_design_summary: One AI-versus-human output comparison reuses AUT responses from 40 Austrian-university students in 20 face-to-face dyads from an October-November 2023 collaboration study and compares them with separately collected responses from 10 chatbots (p. 3, Sections 4.2-4.4). Human scorers assessed fluency, originality, flexibility, elaboration, and the sum of these dimensions, aggregating scores per dyad or chatbot (pp. 3-4, Section 4.5). No human received AI assistance; an AI-supported human experiment is proposed as future work (p. 6, Section 6).

studies.label: Alternate Uses Test: 20 student dyads versus 10 independently tested chatbots

assignment.what_was_assigned: No people were assigned AI assistance in this comparison: existing human-dyad responses were compared with separately collected chatbot responses. The human data came from the face-to-face condition of an earlier collaboration study; dyads were paired using interest profiles. Randomization in that earlier study is not described (p. 3, Sections 4.2-4.3).
assignment.quote: The uses generated by the AI chatbots were collected separately for this study, between January 19th and February 5th, 2024.
assignment.locator: p. 3, Sections 4.2-4.3; p. 6, Section 6 (AI-supported human experiment is future work)

arms.name: Human dyads
arms.description: 40 students analyzed in 20 dyads, brainstorming without generative AI; responses reused from the face-to-face condition of an earlier study (p. 3, Sections 4.2-4.4).

arms.name: AI chatbots
arms.description: 10 chatbots performed the AUT individually using standardized prompts; these are systems, not people, so the human n fields are null (p. 3, Sections 4.2-4.3; p. 4, Table 1).

participants.exclusions: Participant recruitment totals and participant exclusion totals are not stated. Repeated or incomprehensible uses were excluded as invalid, with no number of discarded uses given; these are output exclusions (p. 4, Section 4.5).
participants.who: 40 students at an Austrian university, mostly psychology students, analyzed in 20 face-to-face dyads; the dyads were matched using interest profiles (p. 3, Sections 4.2-4.3).
participants.quote: The 40 human participants were students from an Austrian university (mostly psychology students),
participants.locator: p. 3, Sections 4.2-4.4; p. 5, Table 3 (20 analyzed human dyads)

ai_tool.name_model: Microsoft Copilot (creative mode), ChatGPT-3.5, Bard, Llama2, Pi, Character Assistant, Perplexity AI, Copy AI, Claude (Claude-instant via Poe.com), and Vicuna (Vicuna-13B)
ai_tool.how_used: Chatbots produced their own AUT answers individually, in written English, with standardized initial, repeat, and transition prompts and no preceding conversation. Repeated prompts continued until the human median count per object was reached or surpassed (fork 13, balloon 12.5, key 12), the chatbot refused, or it exactly repeated earlier uses. Responses were collected between January 19 and February 5, 2024. No person received AI help (p. 3, Section 4.2; p. 4, Table 1).

task.description: Alternate Uses Test for fork, balloon, and key. Human dyads brainstormed aloud in German and their responses were transcribed; chatbots responded individually in written English (p. 3, Sections 4.1-4.2).
task.duration: Human dyads: 3 minutes per object. Chatbots: a response-count/refusal/repetition stopping rule; no equivalent time limit is reported (p. 3, Section 4.2).

outcomes.name: AUT fluency
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Two scorers worked independently and resolved differences by consensus; expert qualifications are not stated. Repeated or incomprehensible uses were removed (p. 4, Section 4.5). One point per unique valid use for each object; slight adaptations were accepted. The initial-prompt-only AI result is a variant of this outcome. Repeated prompting to reach the human median limits interpretation of the full fluency comparison (pp. 4-5, Sections 4.5 and 5). Scores were summed across objects to one score per human dyad or chatbot (pp. 3-4, Section 4.5). The 30 observations comprise 20 human teams plus 10 individual chatbots; team denotes the human analysis unit (p. 5, Table 3).

contrasts.reported: Full fluency score: AI mean = 39.500, md = 39.0, sd = 10.50, n = 10 chatbots; human mean = 39.150, md = 37.5, sd = 11.43, n = 20 dyads. Initial-prompt-only AI variant: mean = 26.30, md = 25.5, sd = 10.91. No fluency test statistic or p-value is printed. The full comparison is constrained by prompting AI to at least match the human median counts.
contrasts.locator: pp. 4-5, Section 5, fluency paragraphs; p. 3, Section 4.2 (AI stopping rule)

outcomes.name: AUT originality
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Two scorers worked independently and resolved differences by consensus; expert qualifications are not stated. Repeated or incomprehensible uses were removed (p. 4, Section 4.5). Originality is a category-rarity score over the combined human and chatbot uses: 2 points for a category occurring < 3 times, 1 point for 3-5 occurrences, and 0 points for > 5 occurrences, as printed (p. 4, Section 4.5). Scores were summed across objects to one score per human dyad or chatbot (pp. 3-4, Section 4.5). The 30 observations comprise 20 human teams plus 10 individual chatbots; team denotes the human analysis unit (p. 5, Table 3).

contrasts.reported: Human mean = 23.00, md = 20.5, sd = 9.29; AI mean = 14.50, md = 14.0, sd = 9.90. Mann-Whitney U = 147.0, p < 0.05. Analysis groups: 20 human dyads and 10 chatbots (Table 3); these n values count producers, not people. The workshop paper prints a p-value threshold, not an exact p-value.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section 5, originality paragraph and Figure 1; p. 5, Table 3 (group counts); pp. 3-4, Section 4.5 (aggregation)

outcomes.name: AUT flexibility
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Two scorers worked independently and resolved differences by consensus; expert qualifications are not stated. Repeated or incomprehensible uses were removed (p. 4, Section 4.5). One point for each distinct use category named by a dyad or chatbot per AUT object; subsequent uses within that category receive no additional flexibility points. This measures category range within each producer, rather than similarity across people (p. 4, Section 4.5). Scores were summed across objects to one score per human dyad or chatbot (pp. 3-4, Section 4.5). The 30 observations comprise 20 human teams plus 10 individual chatbots; team denotes the human analysis unit (p. 5, Table 3).

contrasts.reported: Human mean = 34.60, md = 33.0, sd = 9.32; AI mean = 31.70, md = 30.0, sd = 8.67. The text describes the Mann-Whitney difference as non-significant; no numerical U or p-value is printed. Analysis groups: 20 human dyads and 10 chatbots (Table 3).
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section 5, flexibility paragraphs and Figure 3; p. 5, Table 3 (group counts); pp. 3-4, Section 4.5 (aggregation)

outcomes.name: AUT elaboration
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Two scorers worked independently and resolved differences by consensus; expert qualifications are not stated. Repeated or incomprehensible uses were removed (p. 4, Section 4.5). Uses received 0 points for no elaboration, 1 for some elaboration or incomplete explanation, and 2 for a detailed, comprehensible explanation with relevant method, purpose, or context (p. 4, Section 4.5 and Table 2). Scores were summed across objects to one score per human dyad or chatbot (pp. 3-4, Section 4.5). The 30 observations comprise 20 human teams plus 10 individual chatbots; team denotes the human analysis unit (p. 5, Table 3).

contrasts.reported: AI mean = 76.00; human mean = 48.10. Mann-Whitney U = 25.0, p < 0.01. Analysis groups: 10 chatbots and 20 human dyads (Table 3). No elaboration SDs or confidence intervals are printed. The workshop paper prints a p-value threshold, not an exact p-value.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section 5, elaboration paragraph; p. 5, Table 3 (group counts); pp. 3-4, Section 4.5 (aggregation)

outcomes.name: Overall AUT score sum
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Two scorers worked independently and resolved differences by consensus; expert qualifications are not stated. Repeated or incomprehensible uses were removed (p. 4, Section 4.5). Raw sum of the points for fluency, originality, flexibility, and elaboration; this combines category counts and human scoring and is not a standardized effect (p. 5, Section 5 and Table 3). Scores were summed across objects to one score per human dyad or chatbot (pp. 3-4, Section 4.5). The 30 observations comprise 20 human teams plus 10 individual chatbots; team denotes the human analysis unit (p. 5, Table 3).

contrasts.reported: Human dyads: mean = 144.85, md = 154, sd = 41.23, min = 77, max = 240, n = 20. AI chatbots: mean = 161.70, md = 162, sd = 42.21, min = 89, max = 216, n = 10. These are dyad/chatbot score distributions. No overall-score test statistic or confidence interval is printed; direction describes the reported means.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section 5 and Table 3, AUT Score Sum: Human Dyads vs. AI Chatbots; table checked with PyMuPDF text-based extraction

outcomes.name: Use categories occurring only in one output group
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: The analysis identifies use categories present only in the human group or only in the chatbot group. Figure 2 shows absolute group counts; the text reports averages per dyad/chatbot. The analysis concerns the two pooled output sets, not independent idea-level observations or people receiving AI assistance (p. 5, Section 5 and Figure 2).

contrasts.reported: mean_dyad = 7.30 categories; mean_AI = 3.90 categories. These are the text-reported averages of group-exclusive categories per dyad/chatbot. Absolute group counts are plotted in Figure 2 but are not transcribed here. No SD, SE, confidence interval, or test statistic is printed for these means.
contrasts.locator: p. 5, Section 5, paragraph following Figure 2, AUT Categories of Use Occurring Only in One Group

diversity_detail.metric: Count of use categories occurring in one output group but not the other; text also reports per-dyad/per-chatbot averages.
diversity_detail.computed_over: The pooled uses of the human dyads and the pooled uses of the AI chatbots, identifying categories exclusive to either of the two groups.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No uncertainty estimate or test is printed for the category averages.
diversity_detail.notes: AI-versus-human output comparison, question = none. The averages are descriptive; statistics_available = none reflects the absence of a complete mean/SD/n summary or another listed statistical result. This is not a human AI-assistance diversity effect.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: The same AI-versus-human pre-study is summarized in c032 (Bangerl et al., 2025, CreAItive Collaboration), Section 4.1, and is labeled S2 in the c032 form; reference [7] links to this exact workshop PDF. It is not an independent sample from c032 S2 and must be kept separate from c032 S1, the later AI-assisted human experiment. The workshop paper itself reuses the 20 face-to-face dyads from an October-November 2023 study of face-to-face versus video-mediated collaboration, whose title is not given.
sample_overlap.quote: The results of the pre-study, which have been published separately [7],
sample_overlap.locator: c151 workshop PDF, p. 3, Section 4.2; c032 PDF, p. 4, Section 4.1 and p. 15, reference [7]: C:/Dropbox/Research/ai-lab/literature/creativity/Bangerl et al (2025) - CreAItive Collaboration.pdf

eligibility.reason: Separate AI-generated and unassisted human outputs are compared; no people were assigned generative-AI assistance (p. 3, Section 4.2). The analyzed human sample is 40 students in 20 dyads, below 50; the 10 chatbots are systems and do not increase the people count (p. 3, Sections 4.2-4.4; p. 5, Table 3). Two scorers assessed the actual AUT responses and resolved differences by consensus, meeting the output-scoring criterion (pp. 3-4, Section 4.5). An AI-supported human experiment is future work (p. 6, Section 6).

one_line_finding: Comparing 20 human dyads (40 students) with 10 chatbots, humans scored higher on originality (23.00 vs 14.50; U = 147.0, p < 0.05), while chatbots scored higher on elaboration (76.00 vs 48.10; U = 25.0, p < 0.01), with no AI-assisted human condition (p. 3, Sections 4.2-4.3; p. 5, Section 5).
notes: For the five main AUT outcomes, n_units = 30 is the arithmetic total of 20 human-dyad observations plus 10 chatbot observations, each contributing one aggregated score; team identifies the human side of this mixed producer comparison (pp. 3-4, Section 4.5; p. 5, Table 3). For group-exclusive categories, n_units = 2 denotes the two pooled comparison groups (p. 5, Section 5 and Figure 2). The corpus contains 783 valid human uses and 395 valid chatbot uses (p. 3, Section 4.4); the paper separately states 1178 uses in total (p. 6, Section 6). These output counts are distinct from the 40 people and the producer observations. Direct comparisons are limited by spoken German versus written English and by time-limited human responses versus repeated AI prompts (p. 3, Section 4.2; p. 6, Section 6). No standardized effect size is computed; the workshop p-value thresholds are retained rather than replaced by the exact p-values in c032.
